THE BRIDE'S FAREWELL. Farewell Mother ! tears are streaming, Down thy pale and tender check; I in gems and roses beaming. Scarce this sad Farewell may speak Farewell Mother: now I leave thee. (Hopes and fears my bosom swell) One to trust who may deceive me. Farewell Mother ! Fare the well.

Farewell Father! thou art smiling Yet there's sadness on thy brow, Winning ine from that beguiling Tenderness to which I go : þÿ Farewell Father ! thou didst bless me, Ere my lips thy name could tell: He may wound! who can caress þÿine- Father! guardian! Fare the well.

Farewell Sister ! thou art twining Round me in affection deep ; Wishing joy but ne'er divining Why "a blessed bride" should weep Farewell brave and gentle Brother I « Though more dare than words can tell ; All beloved ones, Fare ye well Father 1 Mother! Sister! Broihcr! .'

Extract of a letter from a citizen of Baltimore, dated New Orleans March 1, 183ti. You request me to write in full the resuit of my observations ; but to attempt this Would be to become author at once : no man ot common observation can pass through even the small portion of this " western world" which we have traversed, or see the trade borne by this mighty river and its tributaries and landed upon the Levee here, without feeling astounded and giddy at the irresistible force with which the illimitable greatness of this mighty West is pressed upon the imagination. And then to reflect that she is but a stripling, and her immeasurable resources bul just developing, the margins of her rivers literally begirt by their primitive forests, and the few comparatively inconsiderable spots in cultivation, so recently improved that the trunks of the forest trees are not yet decayed ; that there is literally speaking a boundless expanse with a soil from twenty to sixty feet in depth, perfectly alluvial, and capable of sustaining crop after crop of cither cotton, tobacco, rice, corn, and indeed all the most valuable productions of nature to a boundless extent : a large proportion of this too lying between the parallels of latitude most congenial to the culture of cotton and sugar, (say from 29 to 33 deg.) without a rock or stone to impede its þÿcultivation besides which, the mineral resources of the interior country are equally great, though by no means worked to any thing like an equal extent, nor can they

be, whilst there is so much to be made on smaller investments, and with far less perplexity, in an agricultural or mercantile pursuit. 1 had no conception of the vastncss of the trade for which we are endeavouring to become participants : to see it in figures does not strike the imagination with any thing like the force as actually to see it in motion ; and you will have some idea of the appearance it presents, and also its extent and value, when I inform you that in addition to the great amount of flat and keel boats constantly employed in the transportation of produce and merchandize from and to this port alone, there arc besides more than six hundred steam boats registered, and some of these of immense dimensions, and capable transporting of 4000 bales of cotton . and the number is increasing annually, and so rapidly and at such remote points that it is difficult, or rather it is impossible to obtain an accurate list. Besides these, there are several hundred boats of small dimensions engaged in trading in the upper waters of this river and its tributaries, and which never come so low as this place : then add to all this, the yearly increasing products which are to be sent here by not only the foreign influx of emigration continually pouring in, but also that portion which is continually drawing our atlantic or eastern population, and to which almost every State east of the mountains must liberally contribute for years to come. That all the public improvements from east

to west, made or in progress, together with five times their number, can ever visib'y affect the trade of this place, I have not the smallest idea þÿ there is an ample abundance for all the contending parties ; and after they have completed all the various works now in progress, New Orleans will be found to be the same crowded place of business, and to have marclicd ahead as though no attempt had been made to share her prosperity. þÿ Lould the city be rendered healthy, I do not see any thing to prevent its becoming the first

36&ST331 TraatmtsutaiR ®»®aamitw<&3 atss. commercial emporium in the world. The present condition of the place, and particularly of the streets, is far better than I had conceived þÿ ail the principal streets are well paved, and have either flag or brick side pavements, similar to our own, and I have been informed by some of the most intelligent citizens here, that since these improvements have been completed, the health of the city has visibly improved ; and I see no good cause why, with proper precaution, it will not become comparitively healthy. þÿ Patriot.

Unprecedented Quick Sailing. þÿ Captain Doe, of the mail boat Tickler, after landing the mails here on Saturday morning last, proceeded on to Trinidad, thence to St. Vincent, and arrived here from Kingstown on Wednesday morning last, completing the round in little more than 72 hours, although he remained at anchor in Port of Spain and Saint Vincent 13 hours, reducing the time of completing the trip to 59 hours ! þÿ Grenada Chronicle. The sloop Tickler, Doe, above alluded to, belonging to this port, sailed lor Barbados on Monday night, 11th instant, at 10 o'clock, and returned to this island on the Thursday following (17th) at a quarter to four, p.m., having remained 9 hours at anchor in Barbados. þÿ On Saturday, 19th, at three in the afternoon, she went to Bequia and sailed from there at six o'clock the same evening for Tobago, arrived at Corland Sunday 20th, at three o'clock p. m. left there Monday, 21st, at same hour, and anchored in this port at ten o'clock the following forenoon þÿ thus in the space of seven days and a half, of which time 79f hours were spent in port, she performed the two voyages above stated þÿ being under sail in all four days, four hours and a quarter. St. Vincent Gazette, March 29.

Early Home. þÿ There are few minds so callous as to revisit the scenes of their childhood, without experiencing some emotion, þÿ And whether these are in the crowded city amidst all the coarse and ordinary objects of vulgar life, or in the lonely valley, with its green hills and its gliding streams, the same feelings swell the heart, as the thoughts of the past rush over it ; for they speak to us of the careless days of our childhood, of the gay dreams of our youth, of the transient pleasures oi our prime, of the faded joys of our old age. They speak to us of parents now sleeping in the dust, of playfellows in a far distant land, of companions altered or alienated, of friends become as strangers, of love changed into indifference. They speak to us also, it may be> of time mispent, of talents misapplied, of warnings neglected, ol blessings despised, of peace departed. They may speak to us perhaps of God's holy law slighted, of his precepts coinleinncd, of himself forsaken ; of hearts, aias ! not purified and renewed by that grace which they never sought for : but like the wasted volcano, parched and blasted in their own unholy fires. Fairer scenes alt may have viewed than those on which their eyes first opened ; but in them we behold only the inanimate objects of nature, which, however they may charm the senses, or fill the imagination, yet want that deep and powerful interest, which seems entwined with our existence, and which gives a local habitation and a name so powerful a
mastery over us.

An Italian Bishop. þÿ An Italian bishop struggled through great difficulties, without repining or betraying the least impatience. þÿ One of his intimate friends, who highly admired the virtues which he thought it impossible to imitate, one day asked the prelate if he could communicate the secret of being always easy ? " Yes," replied the old man : " I can teach you my secret with great facility ; it consists in nothing more than making a right use of my eyes " His friend begged of him to explain himself. "Most willingly," returned the bishop. ' In whatever state I am, I first of all look up to heaven, and remember that my principal business here is to get there ; 1 then look down upon the earth, and call to mind how small a place I shall occupy in it, when I die and am buried ; I then look abroad into the world, and observe what multitudes there or who are in all respects more unhappy than myself. Thus I learn where true happiness is placed; where all our cares must end; and what little reason I have to repine or to complain."

I-ucifer Matches. þÿ A friend of ours who was bound up the North Kiver a few days ago, happened to be early on board the Ohio, and so sat himself down on the back side of the boat to read a book. As the bustle increased, and just as the boat was starting, a porter threw down a trunk at his feet took his two shillings of a countryman for his trouble, and hurried ofF. Directly our friend discovered an impression of fire on his olfactory nerve, and looking about, beheld the countryman's trunk smoking like a coal-pit. On being opened, it exhibited a doleful mass. In addition to a quantity of Lucifer matches, the countryman had furnished himself with a quantity of small torpedos which had also exploded, so that the silks and callicoes for the ladies, and the sugar plums for the children, were all in ruins. The affair was hardly over, when our friend walked to another part of the boat, where several gentlemen of his acquaintance were regaling themselves with segars, and behold the pocket of one of them man's trunk! "Mr. was smoking almost as much as the ," said he, "your countrypocket is on þÿfire," and the gentleman pulled out his linen cambric handkerchief, which on coming to the air, blazed up beautifully The friction of throwing a bunch of matches back, into his pocket after taking one to light a segar, had been sufficient to produce an exnlosion. The countryman's matches were exploded by the concussion of throwing down the trunk. In Germany severe laws have been passed a-

gainst the having, making, or using Lucifer matches. From the New York Commercial Advertiser, March 3. St. Croix, West End, Feb. 1. 1830. I have now been about three weeks in this lovely island, breathing its tine air, feasting my eyes upon its rich and beautiful landscapes, and riding my poney over its almost unequalled roads We invalids þÿ some of us look like any thing else þÿ become more acquainted with the island than many of its natives: for before breakfast, and after breakfast, and again after dinner, we are mounted on our ponies, and take the principal roads, or those which wind around among the estates, or the mule tracks, zig-zagging the sides of the hills, as the love of variety or whim directs. We have left business at home, but not our Yankee activity ; þÿ and any discovery of a fine view, or an agreeable object of any other kind, is at once communicated, and gives direction to the next ride. It is now crop time, and we make ourselves acquainted with the boiling houses, and eat cane and new sugar. We are told that the negroes grow fat at this season : and if eating cane can fatten them we can easily believe it þÿ for go where you will, the darkies seem to be seriously employed in little else. þÿ Pass a score of them, leading mules laden with cane, for the mills, and you will see them earnestly engaged in discussing a piece of cane, and sauntering along as if it mattered little whether be and his mule reached the works this week or the next. Look at a team bound homeward from the town ! þÿ the charioteer has probably picked up a load of

fellow- blacks, all busy in grinding cane for their own benefit. Some of us have taken to this kind of provender, in hopes of thriving like the negroes, and that with a zeal which will ensure a fair trial of its efficacy. Last week, our island life was very pleasantly varied birty-day. His majesty of Denmark under I whose government we are now living was born on the 28th of January, 1768, and his good subjects of St. Croix, who seem without exception to be sincerely attached to his government, and to entertain the most respectful sentiments toward his person, assembled on the 28th ultimo at the capital, Christianstied or, as it is usually called, Bass End, (a corruption of Bassin) to shew their loyal ity, and assist in the festivities of the occasion. The American invalid corps at St. Croix, quarters at West End þÿ this end of the island being, in general, pleasanter, of better soil, and more highly cultivated, though the town is smaller and inferior in regard to the peculiar accomodations and excitements of town life than Bassin. Most of us, however, went to Bassin, fto pay our respects to his majesty as being temporarily under his protection in the person of his deputy, the governor general of the Danish Islands The day was ushered in by a royal salute from the fort, of twenty-eight guns. About eleven þÿo clock a. m. the troops of the eastern end of the island, including the regulars, stationed at Bassin, and the militia, to the number, in the whole, of about six hundred, paraded a

short distance to the eastward of the town, and were reviewed by his excellency the governor. Their appearance and evolutions were very fine, but the attention of us Americans was principally attracted to the Brand corps, an armed fire company, as the name imports, composed of colored men, and commanded by colored officers. By colored men,

j&bmse&ihtos a'txs they do not here understand blacks, but men of mixed blood. þÿ his ! corps acquitted itself exceedingly well, and might challenge comparison with any on the parade. Between one and two þÿo clock a levee was held at the government house, which was attended by the civil and military functionaries ot the island in their uniforms, andothergentlemen þÿ among whom were twenty of the American visiters. Wine was served, and the king's health drunk, in the brief but emphatic toast Kon- þÿ gen þÿleve. We had heard too much good of Ins majesty, not to join the rest in wishing the king to live. Let it be that a good king is a happy accident, it the more becomes his subjects to pray for his life. After the toast, the Governor, Gen. von Scholten, w ho has passed some time in our country, and seems to have observed the course of political events there with great shrewdness þÿ came directly to the part of the hall, where we republicans were standing, and received us with a degree of courtesy, which deserves acknowledgement. Among the gentlemen present several wore at their button holes the cross of the order of Dannebrog, and among the rest I was gratified to notice the meek looking Mr. BonhofT, the chief of the Moravian missionaries on the island. The badge, an ornament of knighthood, was in singular contrast with bis plain appearance and meek and gentle manners, but, 1 dare say, knighthood, which now has lost its military character, and is thought a fit reward for skill in physic, or novel writing,

or portrait painting, and is conferred sometimes as appropriately as we give L. L D.s, has rarely been bestowed upon a more deserving man. In the evening a soiree was given by his excellency, to which we w-ere all invited. It was in a beautiful saloon, as brilliant as mirrors, chandeliers, gay uniforms, and red coats, for even judges wear red coats her, could by the celebration of the þÿking s amusement were abundant, and most of the make it. The means of refreshment and assembly were soon drawn ofi from the principal hall to the card table under the galleries, &c. &c. or to the billiard room. A friend and myself wandered round to look at scenes to me at least new, but we soon returned to the saloon, where the governor again gave us his company, and entertained us highly with his conversation and anecdotes. He is evidently a man of much observation and a great deal of practical good sense. The Dansk Vestindisk liegierings Avis, in giving an account of this soiree, mentions the particular attention paid by his excellency to the Americans present, which they are happy in publicly acknowledging. At ten the company reassembled, champagne was furnished, a Danish song, written for the occasion, was sung with great spirit, the þÿking health s was drunk with repeated cheers, and we went home. Not so all. A supper came next, but we had come to see the people and to join them in paying respect to their excellent sovereign. I have alluded to the roads in this island. I suppose that in no country on earth arc they

so uniformly excellent. Wherever we go we find them hard, smooth, and well formed. Indeed, they are principally macadamised, and I recollect no roads which equal them in our country, except the macadamised or gravelled streets in our larger towns. None of our country roads are to be compared with them. The climate is delicious. The thermometer, when it has a fair exposure, range from sevenly to eighty degrees, and it is spoken of as very

remarkable to see it as low as sixty-eight degrees. Yet the heat is tempered with a refreshing breeze from the east, and the houses are so constructed as to admit the free circulation of the air entirely through them, and in the hottest part of the day we are perfectly comfortable in doors, in flannels and a cloth coat. A cloudy sky is unusual, and when the sun is high, its beams are too powerful for strangers to be exposed to, but in the morning and evening, exercise in the open air is delightful, and in a covered carriage may be taken with the utmost comfort at any time of day. Nothing seems wanting for the comfort of invalids. Tropical fruits are in sufficient abundance, and the provision market is ample. I must not be understood to speak of any such locality as Fulton marketþÿ I mean there is plenty to be had, and it will come to you in parcels on the þÿblackies heads, for that is the way in which they tote things here. The fish is excellent and in great variety, and the mutton of the island is hardly surpassed. It is not among the least of the comforts of the invalid, that he can get medical advice, grounded on high scientific attainments, and an experience in the island of fifty years. We see substantial proofs of the salubrity of the island in the amplitude of many of the inhabitants. I know not w here you will find haler and heartier looking men ; and a yankee blacksmith from þÿ down þÿeast, who has followed his vocation in the town for fifteen years, exhibits as much vigor of health, and
as aldermanly dimensions as any of his craft at home. Adieu, till the next opportunity. Yours, &c. VALETUDINARIES.

JERUSALEM. Jerusalem was a ploughed field, and the ground on which the temple now stands, the joint inheritance of two brothers, one of whom was married and had several children, the other lived a bachelor. They cultivated in common the field which had devolved on them the right of their mother. At harvest times, the two brothers bound up their sheaves, and made of them to equal stacks, which they left upon the field. During the night, a good thought presented itself to the younger. þÿ þÿ M> þÿbrother, said he to himself, þÿ has a wife and children to maintain ; it is not just that our shares should be equal ; let me then take a few sheaves from my stack, and secretly add them to his ; he will not perceive it, and therefore cannot refuse them. This project the young man immediately executed. That night the elder awoke and said to his wife. þÿ My brother is young and lives alone, without a companion to assist him in his labors, and console him under his fatigues. It is not just that we should take from the field as many sheaves as fie does ; let us get Up, and secretly go and carry a certain number of sheaves to his stack ; he will not find it out to-morrow, and therefore cannot refuse them ; and they did so accordingly þÿ The next day both brothers went to the field, and ear h was much surprised to find the two stacks alike ; neither being able in his own mind to account for the prodigy. They pursued the same course for several successive nights, but as each carried to his brother s stack the same number of

sheaves, the stacks still remained equal, till one night both determined to stand centinel to elucidate the mvstcry ; thev met, each bearing the sheaves destined for his þÿbrother stack. s þÿ Now, the spot where so beautiful a thought at once occurred to, and was so persevcringlv acted upon by two men, must be a plac e agreeable to Cod ; and men blessed it, and chose it whereon to build a house to His þÿname. How charming is this tradition ! How it breathes the unailccted benevolence of patriarchal morals ! How simple, primeval, and natural, is the inspiration leading men to consecrate to Coil a spot on which virtue lias germinated upon earth ! I have heard, among the Arabs a hundred legends of the same description. The air of the Bible is breathed alt over the East þÿ A De Lamartine's Pilgrimage to the Holy Land.

The debates in Parliament have not yet assumed any remarkable feature of interest. Lord Morpeth, in the House of Commons, gave notice to bring on the Irish Tithe question on the 25th March. The Carlow Election Committee had not yet reported their opinion on the þÿO Connelland Raphael transaction. One thing the Radicals in the House of Commons have succeeded in þÿ the getting rid of Orange Lodges, institutions founded on the basis of loyality to the King, and profound attachment to the Protestant Church, of which the Duke of Cumberland is Grand Master. Mr. þÿHome motion s for an address to the King to put these Lodges down, passed the House, and his þÿMajesty gracious s answer has satisfied the feelings of the enemies of the Church. Instantly, on the intelligence reaching the Duke of Cumberland of the address of the House, and his Royal þÿbrother expres- s sion of feeling on the subject, his Royal Highness took the necessary steps for dissolving all the Orange Lodges. The Church of England is gradually losing her veteran defenders, her unflinching sup-

porters, her brilliant examples of sound learning, and practical holiness. The Bishop of Durham, Dr. Van Mildert, a distinguished man, and great ornament to the Bench, has been called to his rest. Opulent as the See of Durham is, it is said that the Bishop, so princely were his charities, has died comparatively poor. The Ministers, however, mean to reduce the income of the Bishopric considerably. The þÿKing Conge s þÿd elire has passed the great seal requiring the Dean and Chapter to elect Dr. Maltby, Bishop of Chichester, to the vacant See ; a choice this, like some others made by the Whig Ministry, rather ominous to the welfare of the Christian Church. þÿ There are some sad alarming signs in the present day of an apostacy from the Faith þÿ once delivered to the þÿSaints. The splendid luminaries of the Christian world, whose scriptural writings shone with resplendent brightness bv-gone days, in are given up for the ignis fatuus of rational religion. These are, it must be confessed, awful times in which we live. The only paragraph in our London papers having the slightest connection with colonial affairs that we notice is this, that þÿ on the 14th March Lord Glenelg introduced a Bill in the House of Lords for the belter administration of justice in the þÿcolonies, in which we conclude there is a provision made for Chief Judges to preside in our Courts of Justice. By a letter from London hv the Packet wo understand this is certainly in progress. The Chief .1 udge for this island cannot come

too soon. The King has conferred the honor of Knighthood on the following gentlemen : Major General Wiltshire Wilson, R. A., Major General Charles Win. Maxwell, Captains John G. Bremer, Hon. John Ashley Maude, John Stuart Peyton, and Henry Hart, of the Royal Navy, and lias also created a batch of Baronets.

From Texas. þÿ A New Orleans paper of the 15th inst. states that a rumor was abroad, pretty well confirmed, that Santa Anna had by forced marches succeeded in surprising and capturing San Antonio, and that the Texians were compelled to fly to the garrison. þÿ Santa Anna sent orders for an immediate and unconditional surrender, to which the commander of the fort, Colonel Francis, replied that it must be taken by force. There are but about 200 men in the fort, but they are well equipped and provided with stores of every description. Seven hundred more are encamped near the city, and their intention to cut off all supplies from Santa Anna, and unless he be speedily relieved he must be starved into a surrender. Another report confirms the foregoing facts, j i but adds that Gen. Cos is the one who captured the city and not Santa Anna. The main body of the Mexican army, either through disaffection or fear would not enter Texas. Gen. Cos stands now in a most deplorable situation. He had passed his parole d'ltonneur, not to fight against the Texians, and if it be true that he is the capturer of San Antonio, he will doubtless meet little mercy at the hands of his enemies.

Later from Texas. þÿ The steam packet Columbia, Captain Halsey, from Charleston, reached here yesterday, bringing New Orleans papers of the 17th inst., from which we gather the following late and important intelligence of the progress of affairs in Texas. þÿ Information from Matagorda, dated March 10th, states that San Antonio de Behar was besieged by the Mexican army under Generals Sesma and Cos, consisting of forty companies of Infantry, amounting to about two thousand four hundred men, together with fifteen hundred cavalry, under General Filisola, (an Italian) and five hundred mules and baggage. The Texians in the fort, were only two hundred infantry and cavalry, under Colonels Bowie and Travers. The assault on the Fort of Alamo, in the town of San Antonio, commenced Feb. 28th, the Mexicans hoisting a black flag, as indicating no quarters. The New Orleans Bee, adds: þÿ þÿ The garrison being well supplied with eighteen pounders, planted on the fort, made them ply with dreadful eflect, sweeping companies of the assailants before the shot. . The Mexicans surrounded the Fort on all sides; but on all sides were they saluted with its artillery. This continued till 7 o'clock 1. M., when the Mexicans thought proper to evacuate the town, and retire to an encampment within two miles, after leaving five hundred of their comrades slain before the þÿfort. The provisional government of Texas being informed of the contest, an immediate þÿ draft of one third of all Texians capable of

bearing arms was ordered by the acting Governor. But so eager were the Texians in general for their prompt and certain triumph, that when the order reached Matagorda, not one third only but all able bodied citizens, volunteered. Numerous companies were im-

mediately on the march to San Antonio, to drive the Mexicans beyond the Rio Grande, or leave them on the field of hattie. They will act on the offensive in their future operations. We are happy to learn that Doctor Grant is not killed : he, Col. Johnson, and another, were saved. It appears that Grant and some 20 or 30 others had gone out on a scouting party, and had approached too near the invading army They were immediately attacked by a column of the enemy, and only 3 escaped þÿ Grant among the number, exhausted and almost naked; as he was closely pursued by the Mexican cavalry. Yet this is the triumph so bombastically blasoned in the account of the gallant Nicholas Rodriguez, published in the Bee of yesterday. The document was genuine: but we þÿ guessed it was not authentic. The Texians have abandoned Copano, and fortified Labadie or Goliad, higher up. There are now 700 men stationed there, wadi prepared with artillery and ammunition ; and dis- | posed to play checkmate with the wing of the Mexican army, under General IJrrea, lately encamped at San Patricio. The report which we copied yesterday, from the New Orleans Bee of the 15th inst. in relation to the alleged surprise and capture of San Antonio de Bexar, by the Mexicans, is thus confirmed as true in its most essential particulars. Affairs in Texas begin now to wear an alarming aspect, and we may yet expect to hear of some desperate and deadly conflicts. A decree of the Mexican government has been promulgated, declaring the ports of Ma-

tagorda, La Boca, San Louis, Galveston, Brazoria, Harrisburg Goliad, Anahuac, Copauo, and all others on the Texian coast in a state of blockade ; the blockade to commence at the end of ninety days from the 3rd of February. 0 0 (From an Arabian author.) Box-mot of Mahomet. þÿ The best and greatest of men (may God shed upon him copious benedictions') was fond of an occasional joke, but when, in his holy sayings, a facetious remark escaped him, it was never other than the truth, though expressed in an admit and indirect manner. It is related that, one day, he said to an aged female, þÿ At the resurrection, no old woman will be admitted into Paradise þÿ The female, in great distress, exclaimed. þÿ Prophet of God, what have wo poor old women done that we should be excluded from the felicity of entering þÿParadise? The chosen of God (may heavenlv blessings rest upon him 1 ) smiled, and, withdrawing the veil of rubies which covered the pearls of his teeth, said, þÿ The Creator (to whom be glorv !) will make every old woman young again, and then conduct her into þÿParadise.

On one occasion, he had been called upon to marry a couple and after getting them properly arranged, commenced as follows: þÿ Man that is born of woman, hath but a short time to live and is full of þÿmisery, &c. þÿ My dear þÿsir, interrupted the bridegroom, þÿ are you reading the burial service, instead of the þÿmatrimonial. þÿ þÿ Never mind, þÿfriend, whispered the Dean þÿ Vou had better be buried than married þÿ

OT (DAWKS CHRISTIAN STED, Dili MAY 1836. We have been favored with the perusal of London papers to the first of April inclusive pr. Packet, from which we learn that Parliament had adjourned on the 30th March, over the Easter holidays to the 12th of April. The Municipal reform bill for Ireland passed to a third reading in the House of Commons on the 28th March. Ayes. 260 Noes. 199

Majority for Ministers 61 and it was sent up to the Lords ; a bill to amend the municipal reform for England (passed at the last session), was also sent up to the Lords. The occupation of the free republic of Cracow by Russian and Austrian troops, contrary to the treaty of Vienna of 1815, which guaranteed its independence, caused much excitement in England and France ; in both which countries Naval preparations continued, with increased activity þÿ 15 Ships of War were fitting at Plymouth and Portsmouth. þÿ An article from Kiel states that both Sweden and Denmark were arming. The castle of Cronberg is being repaired and strongly fortified, and several Ships of the line to be put in Commission. It is stated that Russia, has added twentysix millions of subjects to her empire within sixty years past, by conquest ; besides an immense territory. Reviews of large corps of the Prussian Army were to take place in May, on the Rhine. The regular army of France, is now 400,000 mcu. It is said the latter power declines the proposal of the British Government to march an army into Spain, to put an end to the barbarous civil war still raging there. A fine French Ship of the line of 84 guns called the þÿ þÿTrocadero accidentally took fire 'in the Roads of Toulon, and vvu1 entirely consumed ; her cost was 3 millions of Francs. Messrs. Rothchild Brothers, had received from the French Government eighteen millions of Francs, being the amount of all the installments now due under the treaty with the

United States ; the residue in two installments, would be paid in 1837 and 1838. The colony of Demerara made 14,000 hogsheads Sugar more, the last crop, than in that of 1831, notwithstanding the apprenticeship system. The duties on East and West India Sugar were to be equalized in G. Britain.

New York papers to 24th April have been received by the Ship Condor Capt. Goodrich, in the fine passage often days from that city. The winter had been the longest and tho most severe, which has been witnessed in the United States since 1780. There was a snow storm in New York 16th April. Tho Ship Condor was fast embargoed by the Ice in Connecticut river from the 1st of December to the 4th of April; the North Biver was not opened to Albany þÿ till the 15th April. The Indian war in Florida was nearly over. The Mexican army had taken St. Antonio De Bexar by Storm, and put the whole Texian garrison to the Sword. Thoughts and Maxims. Madame de Stael has well observed, that men collected in a public assembly, and debating upon great questions of public interest, generally end in electrifying themselves with the marks of mental dignity. Maria Leczinska (Queen of Louis the Fifteenth and daughter of Stanisalus Sobieski, the dethroned King of Poland) frequently remarked, that the mercy of Kings consisted in their justice, but that the justice of Queens was more frequently found in being merciful. Those who reduce every thing to the strictness ol anal) sis resemble chemists, who destroy the splendour and the peifume of flowers, to distinguish theii nature, chui .cier and qualities. A wise man living in a country in a state of revolution, should imitate the traveller who, in passing through a forest inSsed with robbers, makes as little noise as possibh . The Emperor Napoleon often remained, that true wealth does not consist in the possession of gold and silver, but in the judicious use made of them. The English language expresses the Deity more appropriately than any otherþÿ lor God is the contraction of the Saxon good. Every abjuration of love, every oath of fondness, always contains this mental reservation þÿ þÿ so long as you are w hat you now þÿare. True philosophy can discern nothing else in a gieat many, words and names hut the letters of the alphabet which compose them. An active and faithful memory doubles file ; foi it brings a man again upon its stage with all those who have made their exi's.

When a personage becomes iormidable to his competitors, or subordinates, they generally seak to deceive or destroy them. A head properly constituted, can >inmodatc itself to whatever pmov.s liie uci: >itudes ol lortune may place under it. Fools line the hedges which houn the road of life; what can the wise man do out smile as he passes along it ! To do good to our enemies, is to resemble the incense whose aroma perfumes the lire by which it is consumed. To apostles of error are never so dangerous as when they appear in the guise i t grey- headed old men. In the conception of þÿMahomet s paradise, there is no distinction between a pencot woman and an angel. Men are like weathercocks, which are never constant or fixed, but when they arc worn out and rusty. If you have received an injury from any one, wash it out, nut in blood, but in the waters of Lethe. Elevated posts in governments arc like steep rocks, only accessible to eagles and to reptiles. To act upon a determination made in anger, is like embarking in a vessel during a storm. To speak harshly to a person of sensibility, is like striking a harpsichord with your list. Religion and medicine are not responsible for the faults and mistakes of its doctors. Ink is a caustic which sometimes burns the fingers of those who make use of it. An indiscreet person is like an unsealed , , latter, which every body can peruse.

The only really bitter tears arc those which are shed in solitude. An historian should be without passion and without pension. Faith spans the gulf of death with the bridge of hope. There is no richer treasure than a collection of correct and beautiful thoughts and maxims.

Effects of the Frost in Ohio. þÿ An excursion some forty miles north on the Great Miami, has afforded me an opportunity to note the effect of the recent frosts upon vegetation. In many places, the corn and buckwheat are quite injuriously touched, and all other herbage, subject to frost, prostrated. I hiving met with gentlemen from other parts of the State, north to Piqua, cast to Lancaster, the information received from them warrants the conclusion, that the injury has been greater farther north and farther east, than in this vicinity. The tobacco cultivators have, it is believed, suffered severely. þÿ Cincinnati Uaz.

LATE & IMPORTANT FROM TEXAS. Massacre of the Georgia Battalion. The distressing news has reached us of the horrible massacre and butchery of the entire command of Col. Fannin, by the tyrant monster Santa Anna and his forces. Col. F. commanded the Georgia Battalion, and his fall, must consequently carry deep distress and anguish into the bosom of many a bereaved family. Our last advices stated that Col. F. being overpowered by the Mexicans, demolished his fortilieations and fled before the superior foe ; and that in the effort to regain the main body of the Texian Army under Gen. Houston, on the east side of the Colorado river, he had been intercepted by the Mexicans and driven to the Hats. A letter received in this city, by Gen. Bethune from his friend Mr. Lainbpkin who had retired from that country with his family, and wrote from on board a vessel bound to New-Orleans, gives a full and detailed history of the barbarous and inhuman affair. The men under the immediate command of Colonel Fannin, were all killed but five. Among those who escaped were Richard Rutledge formerly of this place, and David I. Holt, from Macon. A party of about 70 under Col. Johnson were cut off, and all put to the sword but four ; our fellow townsman John Love, was so fortunate as to make his escape from the party. Reuben Brown and VV. J. Mitchell of Harris county, Capt. Wads worth and Major Ward, were among the slain all perished during this desperate þÿ battle. The letter further states that Col. Fannin

capitulated upon the promise of Santa Anna, that himself and soldiers should be treated as prisoners of war. But no sooner had this fiend of hell fastened them in his clutches than he secured their arms, and early next morning, ordered them all to be shot. Nero was a merciful man compared with this monster, and the Autocrat of Russia, will blush to read his history P. S. Since writing the above, Gen. Bethune, has very politely tendered us the letter referred to, for publication. The following is a copy. On board schr. DeKalb, ) Mississippi River, April 7. j Dear Sir þÿ You are no doubt somewhat surprised at the heading of this page ; but a few words will explain all. 1 am on board of one of a number of vessels that are laden with the unfortunate, who are flying from the terrors of war. You have perhaps heard of the storming of St. Antonio, &. massacre of the Texian garrison. All without an exception perished, save a woman <St 2 negroes þÿ Davy Crokett was among the number. He had fully sustained his great character for intrepidity, during an unsuccessful attempt of the enemy to storm the Alamo, just one week before the massacre A short time previous to this, a party of sixty or seventy under Col. Johnson, were cut otf, save four. John Love was among the riutnbei who escaped. þÿ Reuben Brown fell here, and young Mitchell of Harris county, fell in the Alamo. The taking of the Alamo was followed by the retreat

Wards worth's company included) had been detached by viol. Fannin, then at Bahia, to protect some families who were flying from the enemy ; when they were attacked, and after fighting and retreating for nearly two days, were at length overpowered five bers, and all put to the sword, but by num- who escaped, and only two of them Georgians; one Richard Rutledge, formerly of Columbus, and the other David I. Holt. In the mean time, Fannin had received orders to abandon the fortress of La Bahia, which he immediately executed, and returned towards the main army with the balance of his troops, 360 men, and seven pieces of artillery, where they were attacked in an open valry. prairie by a large advance A small Mexican force, mostly ca- guard having been but could not tell the result The termina- separated from the main body þÿ saw the fight, tion to this unhappy affair, was explained bv three men who escaped about the time of the catastrophe. Fannin sustained a great many charges in quick succession, sustaining some damage, and doing much execution ; and kept retreating during the tight, which lasted the greater part of a day, until he gained some post oak woods, when the Mexicans ceased their charges, but closely invested the place on all sides. Here Fannin received propositions from the enemy and capitulated upon the

promise of the Mexicans, that they should be treated as prisoners of war. Their arms were immediately secured, and the next morning they were all shot, save the three who escaped. Mrs Fannin had just arrived in Texas, but not in time to see her husband. Many other barbarities have been committed. þÿ The army of Texas after making a stand for a short time on the Colorado, has retreated to the east side of the Brassos. San Phillippe is burnt (by the citizens) and there is a probability that Brazoria and Washing ton have shared the same fate 1 do not expect that there are half a dozen families West of the Brassos. The enemy is known to be marching into the country in two divisions of 2000 men each ; one through the interior upon San Phillippe & the other along the coast towards Velasco. They were momently expected at the latter place when 1 left it, and the advance of the other division had already reached San Phillippe. The Indians had began to be troublesome, and many negroes have runaway þÿ in some instances whole plantations of them had gone off in a body, but had done no further mischief. Very many families and negroes were going eastward, some for the United States by land and by waterþÿ others are making a stand in the east, covered by the army.

LATE NEWS from GENERAL GAINES. The intelligence from the Withlacoochee continues to be of great interest and importance Soon after our last publication we learned that General Gaines continued fighting the Indians. After the battle of the first day Gen.G. found 30 Indians killed. lie had þÿ2 ofhis men killed and several wounded. On the 3d day the Indians crossed the Withlacoochee to attack him. He having taken only 8 þÿday sprovisions, and being thus closely pressed, sent for reinforcements, provisions and ammunition. Gen. Clinch, being under the orders of Gen. Scott, and having received no order to send the provisions for the Army, sent corn from his own plantation, and Mr 15. M Dell started with upwards of 80 head of cattle. For the Journal of Commerce The Old Bachelor as l have found him. When he forms an acquaintance with a lady whom he considers worthy of his notice, he commences an attack upon her heart. 1 1 is first effort is bv special attention, and frequent, well timed compliments, to flatter her vanity. When she speaks, he bangs upon her lips as if they were the fountain of wisdom ; and is surprised that her sentiments coincide so perfectly with his own. It his attentions are not received with a smile of approbation, or not amply returned, he changes his plan ; puts on a countenance indicative of disappointment and the deepest wretchedness, and makes occasional remarks well suited to excite pity, till at length, her heart is melted into tenderness.

This is all he sought ; and in this he glories. He continues to flatter and enjoy, while the novelty lasts, and till he is perfectly satisfied that the conquest is complete and the captive in his power. Suddenly his engagements become numerous and pressing ; he has no time to consult her wishes. His attentions when in her society gradually decline, and at length, to convince her that he did not mean any thing, he gives to some other, in her presence, a decided preference. Her name is added to his list of conquests, and she is left to weep with bitter regret over the benevolence of her heart.

Mr. Editor. þÿ Having read with some surprise and emotion the young Maids complaint against the old Bachelor, I am induced from a strong desire of retaining the good opinion of the fair sex to give a fair statement of the case ; hoping and believing you will oblige a Subscriber by giving it publication. When first introduced to the Complainant, I was truly quite enamoured. Lest you, Mr. Editor, should call in question my good taste, I will give a short description my late Lady loved. of Her figure is rather above the middle size, þÿ full and graceful ; her face oval ; complexion clear and bright ; nose, so, so ; eyes her most attractive feature, dark, large, lustrous, and full of love and sentiment; her mind W'dl informed sensible and shrewd in her remarks, ladylike in her manners. You Sir, would naturally exclaim what more do you want? do you expect perfection ? No, Sir. I will explain why 1 was so inconstant. I found the lady loved herself so much, she could not love another but a very little indeed. But far worse than that, Sir ; she was too fond of admiration. Why, Sir, I never called at her house lint she had Irom half a dozen to- a dozen Beaux around her, and then she sat like a Queen smiling alike on all, not manifesting the least preference lest she might diminish the number of her admirers. This I did not, like, and for this I quitted her. What happiness could a domestic old Bachelor calculate upon from a young wife that was so fond of young men's admiration ! ! I hope I stand

excused in your sight, Mr. Editor and also in the judgment of the Ladies, whom I truly love and esteem, and live in the hope of one happy day calling one of them by the endearing name of Wife. I remain your Obedient Servant. AN OLD BACHELOR;

First Moravian Missionaries. At a missionary meeting in London, in May, 1831, James Montgomery, Esq. of Sheffield, stated, that nearly one hundred years ago, the first missionary fund was formed among the Moravians, or United Brethren. Its amount was indeed small; for when the first two persons offered themselves to go to the West Indies, their patron went with them through (he forest of Lusatia, and when they had come to the verge he comforted their minds, knelt down with them, and commended them to God, and to the word of his grace. When they rose, he said, " Brethren, how much money have you ?" They opened their purses, and showed three dollars ; thirteen shillings and sixpence, if they were Spanish ; or if they were German, only ten shillings and sixpence. He gave them two ducats,

eig hteen shillings, more : so that with about thirty shillings these men went forth to preach the gospel. Such was then the amount of the missionary funds of these good people. Tho thirty shillings thus lent to the Lord, and rested in his service at St. Thomas's, has been so accumulated by providential circumstances, that now the missionary station there, not only supports its own expenses, but has at times realized as much as £300 surplus funds.

DEATH. We are truly sorry to hear of the death of Lieutenant-Colonel John Hastings Mair, K.II# and C T. S , Lieutenant-Governor of tho Island of Grenada. The intelligence of this lamentable event, which took place on the 21st instant, reached this yesterday, per the schooner Carib. The illness of His Excellency, we understand, was of short duration, having been confined only 4 days to his bed. Governor Mair had but recently completed a tour of inspection of the Militia Regiments throughout the Island. The administration of his Government seems to have given great satisfaction to the inhabitants generally, and the amenity of his manners in private life, secured him the good will and esteem of all who enjoyed the honor of his friendship. His loss will, no doubt, he felt in every department of his Government, both public and private.

CHRISTIAN STED, 9th JUNE 1836 Dates from New York to 17th May are received and we regret to add they confirm the massacrees committed by Santa Anna in Texas; he was following up General 7/ouston, who had retreated, but the latter was to be joined by many volunteers, and strong hopes were entertained of his leading Santa Anna into a trap, and taking him and all his army prisoners. Gen. Gaines had also advanced with the U. S. Troops near the theatre of war. Dr. Harrison, murdered by the Mexicans, was travelling in a civil capacity, with three other gentlemen, when they fell in with the barbarians, their bodies were shockingly mutilated. Gen. .Houston had about 2,000 men with him at the last dates, hut volunteers were marching to join him, and it was supposed his force would be doubled in a few days. Propositions are before the Congress of the U. S. to increase the Navy to 15 Ships of the line, 20 frigates, 20 Corvettes, and several Steam Ships, &c. The Texian Schooner Invincible, Capt. Brown, fell in with the Mexican Schooner Montezuma off Brazos De Santiago ; a desperate action immediately ensued, w hich fasted several hours and terminated in the destruction and sinking of the Mexican Schooner, crew and ail.

UNITED STATES AND FRANCE. The following message was received from the President of the United States, by the hand of Asbury Dickins, Esq. and read : Washington, May 10, 1836. To the Senate and House of Representatives : Information has been received at the Treasury Department that the four instalments under our treaty with France have been paid to the agent of the United States. In communicating this satisfactory termination of our controversy with France, I feel assured that both Houses of Congress will unite with me in desiring and believing that the anticipations of a restoration of the ancient cordial relations between the two countries, expressed in my former messages on this subject, will be speedily realized. No proper exertion of mine shall be wanting to efface the remembrance of those misconceptions that have temporarily interrupted the accustomed intercourse between them. ANDREW JACKSON.

A letter from Rome states that Don Miguel, having offered rudeness to the beautiful princes Aldobrandini Borghese, (formerly Miss Talbot) was challenged by the prince, but refused to fight on the plea of superior rank, and that but for the interference of the pope himself he would have been cudgelled by the indignant husband. The insult was offered in the chapel of the Vatican, during the performance of a solemn religious ceremony.

A memorial of a painful and touching Character was presented to the Queen of Spain on the 23d o I March. It was signed by Colonel Don Manuel Frontineras, and stated that his young wife had been shot, with twenty nine other females, by order of the Carlist's chief Cabrera, in revenge for the execution of his mother, shot as a spy.
